observations.text:
When I worked in kids clubs we didn’t just wait for the kids to arrive, and ask them to do the assigned activity. 

If it was pirate day, we dressed like pirates, talked like pirates, played pirate games, made pirate hats and played sea shanties while we worked. 

From the moment kids walked through the door to the moment they left - pirate land. 🏴‍☠️ 

Then, after the session finished, I’d reset the tent, and start building the world for the next day. 

Granted, on a shoe string budget they had to fill a lot of gaps with their imagination, but because we showed up with heart, they met us in the middle. 

Adults… employees… really aren’t much different.

Every detail mattered because every detail reinforced what we were creating. You can’t just look at one touchpoint. It’s all one journey.

Here are three questions you can ask yourself:

🗺️ Is your #EmployeeExperience map a set of moments or a journey?

🦜Does it just look good on paper, or does it actually make your employee feel good?

⚓️ Are your details reinforcing one coherent experience, or creating friction?

The best experiences aren’t built on budget. They’re built on intentionality across every touchpoint. 

🪎🪎🪎

A little bit of extra effort goes a long way.

observations.text:
Why I'll Keep Choosing the Stage

The first time I stood on a stage, I thought I was there to share what I knew.
Years later, after speaking across India, Japan, the Middle East and on platforms like TEDx, leadership conferences and corporate forums, I've realised something.

I was never there just to speak.
I was there to start conversations that continue long after the audience leaves the room.

Over the years, I've spoken about digital transformation, marketing strategy, business growth, AI, leadership and building brands.

But one talk continues to stay with me.
At TEDx, I spoke about the art of knowing yourself.

At the time, it felt like a deeply personal idea.
Today, I believe it's one of the most important leadership capabilities we have.

Because subject matter expertise will get you into the room.
Self-awareness determines how you lead once you're there.

The best marketers don't just understand consumers.
They understand themselves.

The best leaders don't just make decisions.
They understand what drives those decisions.

The best coaches don't just ask powerful questions.
They remain deeply aware of their own assumptions before asking them.

I've spent considerable time building businesses, leading marketing teams, advising organizations and coaching leaders.

If there's one thing those experiences have taught me, it's this:

Knowledge gives us competence.
Self-awareness gives us wisdom.
And leadership needs both.

That's why I'll keep choosing the stage.
Not because I love being seen.
But because I love sharing ideas that help people see themselves differently.

Whether that's a keynote, a boardroom discussion, or a coaching conversation, my hope is always the same:

That someone leaves the room thinking differently than when they walked in.Because sometimes, one new perspective is all it takes to change the way we lead.

What conversation do you believe leaders need to have more often?

observations.author: self
observations.text:
What if self-doubt isn't the problem?

Most leaders, founders, and high performers I coach don't eliminate self-doubt. They simply shorten the amount of time they spend believing it.

The difference isn't the absence of doubt. It's the speed of awareness.

The moment you notice:
➡️ "This is self-doubt talking."
➡️ "This isn't necessarily the truth."
➡️ "I can choose my next step anyway."
That's where growth happens.

I've found that confidence isn't built by never questioning yourself. It's built by learning how quickly you can return to clarity when doubt shows up.

Curious: What helps you move through self-doubt faster when it appears? I'd love to hear your perspective in the comments.

observations.text:
Last week, while supporting a leadership workshop for a luxury retail brand in Dubai, I noticed something.

Leaders often look outside their organisation for answers — through mentors, coaches, or training programmes — when some of the most valuable learning is sitting across the room.

One brand. Different functions. Similar challenges.

Whether you're leading Operations, HR, Finance, Marketing, or Retail, many of the conversations are surprisingly similar: balancing competing priorities within budget constraints, managing teams, navigating expectations and deadlines, leading through change, and delivering results.

At some point, department labels becomes secondary. Leaders realise they're not the only ones carrying those questions. They stop speaking as Heads of Marketing or Operations and start speaking simply as leaders.

Then the conversation changes. Questions become more honest, ideas more practical, and people begin learning from one another.
Often, the most valuable insight doesn't come from the facilitator. It comes from someone across the table who's been navigating the same challenge from a different function.

Leadership grows faster when people stop learning in silos and start learning from one another.
Sometimes the expertise you're looking for is already in the room.

observations.author: self
observations.text:
Striving vs. arriving

I found today moving straight from one completed goal to the next — and I suspect I am not alone.

In high-performance environments, striving is a strength. We set goals, deliver, and keep going:
• “I’ll relax when this project is done.”
• “Let’s push to the next milestone.”
• “What’s the next move?”

But the goalposts rarely stay still.

Psychology shows we rapidly normalise achievement — the hedonic treadmill at work. What once felt significant quickly becomes the baseline.

In many organisations, striving is visible. Arriving is not.

Without moments of arrival, work (and life) can start to feel like a race with no real sense of progress.

Pausing matters. Reflection supports memory consolidation and strengthens self-efficacy. In simple terms, the brain needs a moment to register “this mattered” for it to translate into confidence, learning, and fulfilment.

We assume people will feel achievement once they reach it — in reality, they often don’t.

If striving drives performance, arriving is what makes it sustainable.

I have been partnering with individuals to work towards their goals, dreams and aspirations. I use a holistic approach to coaching that is fully directed by what the client would like to achieve. This incorporates Co-Active coaching where it is truly believed that the individual holds all the answers even if unaware of such. I have partnered with individuals who are going through transitions personal or career based and required clarity and guidance during this time. I have also supported individuals going through grief and loss using coaching approaches. This is an area I am passionate about as I have seen/experienced first hand the difference appropriate support can have at these times.

Previously I was a Nurse with over ten years experience in different fields when my nursing journey came to an end. It didn't help that I hurt my back so my abilities in Nursing practices were more limited then what they once were. What had the greatest impact though was moving abroad firstly to the middle east, then Asia, back to the middle east and finding I was unable to maintain an equivalent role whilst balancing being a mother of three. 

When the Nursing door closed something felt like it was missing. I was no longer helping or caring for individuals outside of family and friends. How could I use all these people skills such as active listening, team work, problem solving that I had mastered during my Nursing days? I asked myself how can I truly care for and support people at this current moment that aligns with my values? 
Coaching then presented itself, something that I hadn't really considered before but yet aligns well with my true inner self. I then started on my coaching journey to become the best coach I can be. I undertook a level 2 coaching course and haven't looked back. 

I believe in coaching in a holistic, client centered manor, underpinned by truly caring about the individuals needs in a non judgmental fashion. This in itself I can see the links between my nursing days with holistic patient centered care and how I apply this to each of my coaching sessions.
From this 'The Self Project' was born where my aim is make coaching as easily accessible for all as possible. Where perhaps coaching was once out of reach to an individual.

One thing that always fascinates me when we explore Emotional Intelligence is what happens when leaders stop analysing everyone else and start analysing themselves 💡 

One pattern emerged again and again.

Leaders rarely struggle to recognise the impact of other people's behaviour.

Recognising the impact of their own is much harder.

Not because they don't care.

But because we're all too close to ourselves.

🔍 One of the most powerful discussions centres around Intention vs Impact.

🎯 What the leader intended
 "I know what I meant."

👥 What the team experienced
 "My team only experiences what I do."

Those two things aren't always the same.

🎯 A leader may believe they're being decisive.
👥 Their team experiences them as dismissive.

🎯 A leader may believe they're staying calm.
👥 Their team experiences silence as disinterest.

🎯 A leader may believe they're empowering people.
👥 Their team experiences a lack of support.

That's why self-awareness isn't simply the starting point of Emotional Intelligence.

It's the starting point of leadership.

Leadership isn't measured by your intentions.

It's experienced through your impact.

An AI audit is not a smarter version of an IT audit. 
It is a different thing entirely.
In a traditional IT audit, I know what I am looking for. Controls. Access logs. Change records. Configuration standards. The system either complies or it does not.
With AI, the system makes decisions. And auditing a decision is fundamentally different from auditing a setting.
I cannot just check whether the model is running. 
I need to understand what it was trained on, what it was designed to optimise for, whether the outcomes it produces are fair and explainable, and whether the humans relying on it actually understand what it is doing.
That is a much harder audit. 
And here is the part that matters most.
It cannot sit with the auditors alone.
The data team owns the training data. 
The business owns the use case. 
The technology team owns the infrastructure. 
Leadership owns the risk appetite. 
Everyone has a piece of this.
An AI audit without shared ownership across all of those functions will find symptoms and miss causes.
This is why AI governance is not an audit problem. It is an organisational accountability problem that audit has to shine a light on.
Is your organisation clear on who owns AI accountability?

I once received a list of five projects that had already started.
No budget approved. 
No resources assigned. 
No PMO involvement. 
Just five initiatives quietly in motion, driven by good intentions and the confidence that someone, somewhere would sort out the details later.
They came to me when the details refused to sort themselves out.
I have seen this pattern more times than I can count. 
A business leader gets excited about an idea. 
They start moving. 
The PMO feels like a gate, not a door. 
So they go around it.
What they do not realise is that the PMO is not there to slow things down. 
It is there to make sure the thing they are excited about actually happens. Budget. Resources. Dependencies. Risk. 
Priorities across the portfolio. 
Without that structure, even a great idea runs out of road.
Three of those five projects were cancelled within a year. 
Not because the ideas were bad. 
Because they were built on air.
The PMO is not a bureaucracy. 
It is the scaffolding that holds the building up while you construct it.
Does your organisation treat the PMO as a gateway or a guardrail?

My contribution is entitled “In a BANI World, the Leadership Superpower That Shouldn’t Be Ignored.” The world? In a state of constant change and challenge. The superpower in question? Humour.

And no, I don’t mean “share a fun fact” humour. And please no one become David Brent from The Office. Humour in leadership is giving yourself permission to name the absurdity everyone in the room already feels, but nobody’s said out loud. It’s holding something lightly when the stakes are highest. It’s not just comic relief. It’s emotional intelligence with better timing.

I’ve seen both sides of this. When I trained as a lawyer I was told, within months, to “tone it down.” I later worked somewhere that treated fun as a genuine value and watched it change everything: how people spoke up, how teams solved problems, how well things held together under pressure.

And it’s not just anecdotal. There’s neuroscience and research which shows us the positive impact of fun and humour in the workplace. It’s not just a fun idea, it’s factual. 

Credibility gets you in the room. Humour gets you trusted.

Thanks to Faith Mneno (MBA) and the TedX Al Wasl team for including me.

Link to my article and the rest of the brilliant magazine in the comments.. how have your seen humour work well in leadership? 

#TEDxAlWasl #Leadership #HumourAtWork #TheHOWWay

observations.text:
Meet Anna.

Successful key account manager. Promoted to a new internal marketing role. New content. New team to lead.

She was used to having all the answers. To having her team's trust. To overdelivering on every KPI.


Then suddenly she needed to ask her new team and new supervisor how things actually ran.

Which she was reluctant to do. She didn't want to look like she didn't know.

Which led to a performance dip, because she didn't know the full spectrum of the work she was now responsible for.

Which led to a trust issue, because she wasn't open about what she needed. Not to the team. Not to her manager.

Same company. New role. The Change Curve in action.


And this is exactly what most people miss when they hear "career transitions coach". They assume I help people leave their jobs. Or change careers completely. Yes, I do that, too. But many transitions I work with don't involve leaving anywhere.

- A promotion that doubled the scope overnight.
- A new manager whose unspoken rules you haven't learned yet.
- Returning from parental leave to a team that moved on without you.
- A relocation with the same company logo on the badge.
- Moving from expert to leader. Same desk, completely different job.
- A restructure where the only thing you kept is your pay grade.

Same employer. Same building. Sometimes the same chair. Everything else has shifted.

These transitions get overlooked because nothing about them looks like one.

- No proper farewell drinks. 
- No handover document for who you used to be. 
- No first day, because technically there isn't one. 

You show up on Monday and start performing in a role that hasn't fully arrived yet - while still half-attached to the one you've just left.

That's transitions as well. Inside careers. The ones nobody quite notices. Including, very often, the person going through them.

A CEO once told me his strategy was perfect. His hands were shaking.
That gap — between what leaders say and what their bodies already know — is where I've spent the last decade. 

Over 10,000 coaching sessions across four continents, sitting across from executives, diplomats, and leaders whose decisions shape organizations and communities. What I found changed how I coach: the body arrives at the truth before the mind does. Not as metaphor. As observable, repeatable fact.

I built a methodology around this. Somatic Thinking is how the body processes what words haven't caught up to yet. The Arabic word for self — النَّفْس — includes the body, the breath, and the soul in one concept. No English word holds all three. That's where this work begins.

The ICF accredited it. Coaches from 13 countries across four continents now practice it. The methodology is Islamically grounded and globally practiced — a framework that didn't borrow from the West but emerged from a tradition that has studied presence, intention, and the body for over a thousand years.

I work with: 
- Leaders and organizations navigating decisions under pressure — when the playbook runs out and the body is the only honest signal left.
- Coaches who sense their toolkit is incomplete — who want to work with the body but were never taught how. 

The Somatic Thinking Coach Education (STCE) is where that changes.
I also speak, write, and occasionally make people laugh in three languages. First Arab to hold the ICF Master Certified Coach (MCC) credential. ICF Young Leader Award 2019.

Curious? Message me — I read every one.

—

Surrender is not a beautiful idea about letting go. It is what your hands are holding and refuse to release.

Eid asks one honest question: what am I still gripping that was never mine to keep?

May this Eid bring you closer to yourselves.

I welcome you in my session today about sensory observation in coaching hosted by ICF Doha Chapter

جلستَ يومًا أمام من تُرافقه، وسمعتَ نفسكَ تسأل: «أين تشعر بهذا في جسدك؟» — وخطر في داخلكَ سؤالٌ لم تنطق به: هل كنتُ أُصغي، أم كنتُ أقود؟
هذا التردّد ليس خللًا في حرفتك؛ إنّه العلامة التي تفصل بين الاستنتاج والإتقان في مستوى MCC، ومُقيِّمو الاعتماد يشعرون بالفرق قبل أن يُسمُّوه. لم تكن هذه ثغرةً فيك، بل في الطريقة التي قدّمت بها صناعةُ الكوتشينج الأسئلة والعملَ الحسّي — أسئلةً تُحدِّد مواقع الجسد، لا انضباطًا في الملاحظة.

في تسعين دقيقة، يُشاركك سامر حسن، MCC — أوّل عربيٍّ يحمل الاعتماد — طريق وطريقة الملاحظة الحسّية، لتحلُّ محلّ السؤال الرتيب الذي يُحدِّد موقع الجسد. نمرُّ معًا على بروتوكول الحضور في أربع خطوات، و تفسِير لماذا تسبق إشارةُ الجسد الجملةَ، ونختم بعرضٍ حيٍّ لخمسة دقائق من الكوتشنج مع زميلٍ من القاعة. تُغادر ببطاقة تطبيقٍ واحدة، بين زملاءٍ اختاروا العُمق على السرعة. 

انضمّ إلينا في هذه الجلسة المجّانية التي يستضيفها فرع ICF الدوحة خلال أسبوع الكوتشينج الدوليّ 2026. لا تستطيع الحضور مباشرةً؟ سجِّل على كلّ حال — يصل ملخّصُ الجلسة وبطاقة التطبيق إلى كلّ مسجِّل.

You have sat across from a client and heard yourself ask, “Where in your body do you feel that?” — and a part of you quietly wondered whether you were listening, or leading. That hesitation is not a flaw. It is the signal that separates deduction from mastery at the MCC level — and ICF assessors feel the difference before they can name it. This gap was never yours to carry. The industry taught somatic work and inquiry as a set of body-locating questions rather than as a discipline of observation.

In ninety minutes, Samer Hassan, MCC — the first Arab to hold the credential — will share the observation stem that replaces the usual body-locating question, the four-step presence protocol that precedes it, and a live five-minute coaching demonstration with a colleague from the room. You leave with one page you can apply in your next session, in a room of coaches who chose depth over speed.

observations.text:
There is a lot of advice about becoming a better version of yourself.

Build better habits. Wake up earlier. Stay consistent. Be more productive. Be more disciplined. And yes, these things matter. They help us grow when life is stable and the goal is continuous improvement.

But life doesn't always ask for a better version of who you already are.

Sometimes it asks you to become someone different.

A new role. A major setback. A career transition. A loss. A leadership position you never felt fully ready for. These moments cannot always be solved by working harder or optimizing your routine. They require letting go of old ways of thinking, old identities, and sometimes even the version of yourself that brought you this far.

That is often the hardest part of growth.

Real transformation isn't about adding more. It's about creating space for something new to emerge.

As a coach, I've seen this many times. The breakthrough rarely comes from finding the perfect strategy. It happens when people stop asking, "How can I do more?" and start asking, "Who do I need to become to lead this next chapter of my life?"

Growth is not always about improving yourself.

Sometimes it's about reinventing yourself.

Trust with others requires self-trust first.

That is one key takeaway from the last Thoughts Leaders Breakfast Club I attended.

We often speak about trusting others, but our capacity to do so is shaped by something deeper: our relationship with ourselves.

Self-trust is built on two foundations: self-awareness and self-confidence. Self-awareness helps us understand who we are, what we value, where our boundaries lie, and why we react the way we do. Self-confidence gives us the energy to act and engage in alignment with that understanding.

When those two come together, we stop trying to become who the world expects us to be and start becoming who we are meant to be.

That’s why I dedicated an entire chapter of my book, Become Who You Are Meant to Be, to self-awareness. In my own experience coaching leaders, it is the gateway to clearer decisions, greater emotional steadiness, stronger relationships, and ultimately, finding the path that is uniquely ours.

Thank you, Azizah Crane  and Dave Crane  for creating a space for a conversation that reminded us that trust is not only something we extend to others, it is something we cultivate within ourselves first.

What if the real question is not how talented your people are, but how they naturally create impact?

The key message in Michael Short ‘s post is powerful:

Sustainable business growth does not come from talent alone, but from understanding how people naturally channel their energy, passion, and potential into meaningful team impact.

For those of you who don’t know about the GC Index, it’s an organimetric tool used by the business/operations/leadership side of a business to understand where the energy of impact for each individual comes from and how these energies interplay in projects, and teams within the larger organization.
 
www.thegcindex.com

As a GCologist myself (certified to administer, interpret and coach to the GC Index), what I value most about The GC Index is that it moves us beyond the usual questions of personality, behavior, or style.

It asks a sharper question:

How does this person naturally create impact?

That distinction matters.

Because in high-performing teams, growth does not come only from hiring talented people. It comes from understanding how each person contributes energy, influence, creativity, execution, strategy, and momentum in different ways.

When leaders understand that, they stop trying to make everyone contribute in the same way. They start designing teams where different proclivities complement each other, and where people are positioned to bring their best impact forward.

But I fully agree with the key point made by Michael: the tool is not the transformation.

The real work happens when data is interpreted with care, translated into coaching conversations, and embedded into leadership behavior, team rhythms, and decision-making.

That is where team performance moves from individual effort to collective intelligence.

And that is where arithmetic contribution can become geometric growth.

Great post and an important reminder for any organization serious about scaling people, culture, and performance.

DM me if you want to learn more about how the GC index tool and methodology can help your organization leverage the natural energy for impact from all it’s constituents.

Strange experience at Lenskart a few days back in Kolkata. I walked in and asked for a spectacle cleaner - the liquid spray used by those who wear glasses. So there’s an offer and I could get two for approx 1.3 times the price of one. Fair enough. 

So I asked if I could get a couple of the soft cloths. Again, something that those who wear specs will understand. 

Apparently not, for in lenskart, those are available ONLY if you purchase the full frame and lenses. I was silent, wondering what level of customer service this was meant to be - because upselling it certainly wasn’t. 

And then in order to generate a bill, the salesman wanted my mobile number. This I positively avoid nowadays since it results in spam of the highest order. No, the gent says, I need to send the invoice there. 

Don’t worry, I said, I can do without an invoice. 

No, but I can’t even generate an invoice without a number. 

So I said ok, put +911234567890

Oh no, he says I need a real number. 

I said, calmly, ok. I’ll go to GKB. 

And walked out. 

#musingsofamorning #lenskart #customerservice

Many people think about their career only when something forces them to—redundancy, burnout, restructuring, AI, or a changing job market.

But today's careers are rarely linear. They need to be designed, not left to chance.

If you are thinking about your next move, these four questions are a good place to start:
1. Know yourself.
 What are your values, strengths and transferable skills? Which parts of your work give you energy, and which drain it?
2. Know where you are heading.
 Do not just think about your next role. Think about the experiences, skills and impact you want your career to build over time.
3. Learn from others.
 Talk to people whose careers you admire. Their journeys are often far less linear than they appear—and that is where the valuable lessons are.
4. Keep learning.
 Career pathing is not a one-time exercise. As industries evolve and new opportunities emerge, your career should evolve with them.

Whether you are changing careers or growing within your current organisation, the most fulfilling careers are rarely accidental. They are built through intentional choices, continuous learning and the courage to adapt.

If your career were starting again today, what would you do differently?

HR Transformation in the Age of AI
AI is no longer an external capability being integrated into HR.
It is becoming the architecture HR operates on.
I completed the “Reimagining HR in the Age of AI” program with the LEORON Institute in Abu Dhabi, focused on the shift from digitised HR functions to AI-enabled operating models, and an intro on Agentic AI

The distinction is becoming increasingly clear in practice:
- AI is reshaping how workforce capacity is structured, not just how it is managed
- Capability planning is moving from periodic cycles to continuous systems (always on and ready)
- Leadership decision-making is increasingly dependent on real-time organisational intelligence rather than static reporting

Within this context, HR is no longer evolving through tools or frameworks. It is being redefined through the design of operating models.

The most material constraint I am observing across organisations is not the adoption of AI itself, but the ability of legacy HR structures to absorb system-level change at the pace required by business transformation.

That is where the work now sits.

observations.text:
He told me he'd put a note in his calendar. 6PM. A reminder about a conversation we'd had years ago.

I only found out because he'd quietly started engaging with my posts again, and when I reached out, he mentioned the note.

I have done this work a long time.
That still made my whole month.

We got on a call. He's running a team of fifteen now, in an industry rewriting itself every few weeks. A few years ago he was an IC. Then two. Then six. Then fifteen. The only team ahead of forecast while companies around him cut staff.

Then he said the thing that made me sit up.

"I'm just trying to keep my head down and keep delivering."

Here's the question I'll ask you too:

If your head is down and you're delivering… how is that any different from what anyone else can do?

Delivering is not the edge anymore. A machine can deliver. The work that used to make you special is becoming the work that gets automated.

So what's left?

Not the doing. The being. The relationships. The thing humans crave more precisely because everything around them is turning into a screen.

He got it immediately. "What got me here won't get me there."

The job had changed underneath him. Nobody hands you a memo when that happens.

One week, three different people cried in their one-on-ones. Not because of work. Because life walked in. A parent dying. A cancer diagnosis. A marriage ending.

Fifteen humans, fifteen lives, all landing on the desk of the person who used to just… do the work.

Nobody warns you about that part when they promote you.

So we talked about the harder shift. Not strategy. Identity.

When you set the bar at genius level, people stop applauding the good days. They expect the goals. Every time. And the only way to keep taking real risks under that weight is to be willing to be vulnerable.

No vulnerability, no courage. No courage, no edge.

He's the kind of leader who remembers birthdays. Who notes that a colleague's son had surgery so he can ask about it next time. Who opens with the personal question, not the status update.

He does this already. And still said: "I think I could do it even more."

That sentence is why he's going to be fine.

We talked about being nice vs. being kind.

Nice is easy. Nice is "so good to see you" when you both know it isn't quite true.

Kind is harder. Kind tells you what you need to hear and still has your back in the room where you're not present.

His words: "It's very tempting to be nice. But it has a very low ceiling."

So here's what I'll leave you with.

Who do you want to BE in three to five years?

Not what you want to have. Not where you want to live. Who.

No layoff, no market, no algorithm can take an identity away from you. The salary, the title, the house… just functions of who you decided to become first.

He's sitting with that now. The gap between the leader who keeps his head down and the one who lifts it up.

I don't think the answer is finished yet.

But I can't wait to hear what he comes back with.

“If I stop being the person everyone depends on, what value do I bring?”

She had built her career by being dependable

The one who fixed things

Stayed late

Held the team together

It looked like strength

So when the next level asked her to delegate

Step back

Let others find their own answers

She found it uncomfortable

Not because she lacked leadership ability

But because she had spent years proving her worth by being needed

And now growth was asking her to become less essential in the old way

This is a pattern I often notice in coaching conversations

People do not always resist the next level because they fear responsibility

Sometimes they fear losing the identity that made them successful

The reliable one

The fixer

The person who never disappoints

But leadership is not always about carrying more

Sometimes it is about creating enough space for others to carry it too

The hardest part of growth is not always learning something new

Sometimes it is letting go of the version of you that once made you feel safe

The framework I use to understand why some Senior Managers become Directors... while others stay stuck.

Every month, I speak with Senior Managers who ask me the same question.

"I've consistently delivered results for years. Why am I still being overlooked for Director roles?"

Most of them expect me to review their resume.

Or optimize their LinkedIn profile.

Instead, I ask them a different question.

"If your name came up in your organization's next Talent Review meeting... would leadership unanimously agree that you're ready?"

That question changes the conversation.

Because promotions at senior levels aren't based on performance alone.

They're based on leadership confidence.

Over the years, I've realized that leadership is subconsciously evaluating professionals across five dimensions.

I call it the Leadership Confidence Index™ (LCI).

L  Leadership Capability

Can you consistently operate at the level above your current role?

Not once.

Not when it's convenient.

Consistently.

C  Cross-Functional Influence

Is your impact known only within your team...

Or have you built credibility across functions, stakeholders, and business leaders?

Because enterprise roles demand enterprise influence.

I  Impact Narrative

Can you articulate your value in terms of business outcomes?

Or do you still describe your work as tasks completed and projects delivered?

Senior leaders don't promote activity.

They promote business impact.

J  Judgment

When uncertainty arises...

Would leadership trust your decisions without needing to step in?

Because the higher you grow, the less you're promoted for execution...

and the more you're promoted for judgment.

I  Intentional Visibility

Do the people involved in succession planning actually know who you are?

Or is your excellent work still hidden inside your function?

Visibility isn't self-promotion.

It's making sure your leadership is visible where it matters.

Here's the interesting part.

Most Senior Managers score highly in Leadership Capability.

But promotions are often delayed because of the other four.

Not because they're underperforming.

Because leadership doesn't yet have enough confidence to place them in a bigger role.

And that's a very different problem to solve.

The next time you wonder...

"Why didn't I get promoted?"

Don't just ask...

"Did I perform well?"

Ask yourself:

Does leadership trust my judgment?
Do I influence beyond my team?
Have I built credibility across the organization?
Can I clearly communicate my business impact?
Am I visible to the people who shape succession decisions?

Because promotions aren't awarded to the most hardworking professional.

They're given to the leader the business is most confident betting on.


Looking at the Leadership Confidence Index™, which pillar do you think is the biggest blind spot for most Senior Managers aiming for a Director or VP role?

👇 I'd love to hear your perspective.

You are experienced, capable and performing well.


But perhaps you have reached a point where hard work is no longer creating the career movement you expected.

You may feel stuck at the same level, overlooked for promotion or unsure how to communicate the value you bring.

 You may be preparing for a performance appraisal, considering your next leadership move or questioning how to become more visible without feeling overly self-promotional.


This is where I support you.


I am a Career and Leadership Positioning Coach working primarily with mid-to-senior women who want to:


• clarify their next career move


• position themselves for promotion or broader leadership roles


• communicate their achievements and leadership value


• prepare for performance and career-development conversations


• build stronger internal and external visibility


• strengthen their executive presence and professional brand


My own career journey shapes how I approach this work.


I spent several years in educational operations, progressing into a secure senior role. 


I could have continued moving to the next level in that field, but I became intentional about asking whether I could see myself on that path for the next several years.


When the answer was no, I decided to disrupt the expected flow of my career.


While continuing to work, I studied after office hours, practised coaching, attended sessions and gradually gained the experience and exposure required to move into a new professional space.

I was not running away from an unsuccessful career. I was intentionally building one that reflected the work I wanted to grow into.


Today, as a PCC-credentialed coach, I support professionals through my work with LHH and Hult International Business School.


I understand that career success is not always about finding another job or moving into the next available title. Sometimes it is about gaining clarity, being recognised differently and becoming more intentional about how you move forward.

My belief is simple:


Strong performance builds credibility. Clear positioning and strategic visibility create career movement.

I help women move from being known as reliable performers to being recognised for the leadership value they are ready to bring.
